newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten joins war of words over Hong Kong laws.
newsitem.headline: Patten joins war of words over Hong Kong laws.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Thursday ridiculed proposals by a Beijing-controlled panel to roll back the territory's laws on civil liberties and elections once it returns to China's control.
While Patten heaped scorn on the proposals, Beijing fired a salvo at British protests against them.
In a special address to Hong Kong's Legislative Council, Patten flung past remarks praising Hong Kong's civil liberties back in the faces of those who now support China's desire to dilute them.
He named five members and quoted them as extolling Hong Kong's Bill of Rights in debates that led to the chamber passing it unanimously in June 1991.

"Ronald Arculli said it didn't go far enough," Patten said. He also quoted Maria Tam, Selina Chow, Edward Ho and Paul Cheng -- all of whom were selected to the Provisional Legislature China intends to install in place of the elected Legislature upon the handover at midnight on June 30, 1997.
"There is a difference between an about-turn and a revolving door," Patten said. "People in Hong Kong are going to have to stand up for their existing way of life."
The interim chamber, expected to enact the proposed legal revisions, will meet on Saturday to select its chairman and set procedures.
It will sit across the border in China where it will be safe from a legal challenge from Hong Kong's democratic lobby, which argues it is unconstitutional.

Fears that China might embark along the track of reversing recent legislation have arisen since Beijing reacted with fury to democratic reforms spearheaded by Patten, who arrived in 1992 to lead Hong Kong to the changeover.
China's decision to replace the body that was elected in 1995 under the auspices of the Patten reforms was regarded by many as the first step.
China argues that some clauses in the human rights ordinances conflict with the Basic Law, the post-1997 constitution for Hong Kong promulgated by Beijing in 1990.
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang warned China it risked unnerving foreign investors.

"If you can't convince the people of Hong Kong, people may take to the streets, some may keep their frustration in their hearts, some in the civil service may quit. Some may emigrate," he told the South China Morning Post newspaper.
"Investors are similar. They talk about substance (of the laws). If they are happy with it, they will invest more. If they aren't, they will leave," Tsang was quoted as saying.
Britain lodged a strong protest with China on Wednesday over Beijing's proposals.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesman responded by accusing the British of interfering in China's affairs.
"We cannot accept the British protest. It is also totally unreasonable and the so-called protest is unwise," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing.
A Chinese envoy to Hong Kong blamed the British action on Patten, whose reforms resulted in a chill in Sino-British relations in the countdown to 1997.

"This was an angry act by Chris Patten who was ashamed that his long-time confrontation with China had been unfruitful," Zhang Junsheng, deputy director of Xinhua News Agency, China's de facto diplomatic mission in Hong Kong, told reporters.
